questions.question: A nurse presses two fingers to a boy's wrist and feels a steady throb, about 80 times a minute. Each throb comes from one beat of his heart. What does the heart do with each beat?
questions.answer: It pumps blood around the body
choices: It pumps blood around the body
It makes new blood for the body
It cleans waste out of the blood
It makes energy for the body
questions.context: The heart is a muscle about the size of a fist, and each beat squeezes blood out through tubes to every part of the body; the throb at the wrist is that push arriving. Blood is made in the marrow inside the bones, not in the heart, and other organs clean waste out of it.
questions.grade_note: The heart as the pump that sends blood round the body is the first fact of the circulatory system, taught by Core Knowledge at grade 4 and reviewed in 5th-grade body units (map line G5.L6).

questions.question: Blood never stops moving. It flows through tubes that reach from the top of the head to the tips of the toes. What job does the blood do?
questions.answer: It brings oxygen and food to each part
choices: It brings oxygen and food to each part
It carries air from the nose to the lungs
It breaks down food into tiny pieces
It carries signals along the nerves
questions.context: Blood picks up oxygen in the lungs and digested food in the small intestine, and brings both to every part of the body; on the way back it carries away wastes such as carbon dioxide. Air reaches the lungs down the windpipe, food is broken down in the stomach and intestines, and signals travel along the nerves.
questions.grade_note: Blood as the carrier of oxygen and food to the whole body is the core of 4th- and 5th-grade circulatory units (Core Knowledge G4, map line G5.L6).

questions.question: The body's cells break down their food to get energy, and a waste gas is left over. Blood carries the gas to the lungs, and each breath out gets rid of it. Which gas is it?
questions.context: Cells use oxygen to break down their food, and carbon dioxide is left over; the lungs pass it from the blood into the air breathed out, while oxygen goes the other way. Nitrogen makes up most of the air, but it comes back out in about the same amount as went in. Carbon monoxide is a different gas, a poison given off when fuel burns badly in stoves, fires and engines.
questions.grade_note: That the lungs take in oxygen and give off carbon dioxide is the basic fact of the respiratory system in 4th- and 5th-grade body units (Core Knowledge G4, map line G5.L6).

questions.question: A swallowed bite of food slides down a tube into a stretchy, muscular organ. There, juices full of strong acid soak it, and the organ's walls churn it into a thick soup. Which organ is it?
questions.context: The food pipe carries each swallowed bite straight down to the stomach, a stretchy bag of muscle. Its acid juices and churning walls break the food into a thick soup, which then moves on to the small intestine.
questions.grade_note: The stomach and its job of breaking food down are among the main organs every 5th-grade body unit names (map line G5.L6; Core Knowledge teaches the digestive system from grade 2).

questions.question: After the stomach, the soupy food moves on into the small intestine, a long tube coiled up inside the belly. What happens to most of the digested food there?
choices: It is soaked in strong acid
It is made into solid waste
It is stored until it is needed
questions.context: The lining of the small intestine is covered in tiny finger-like bumps called villi, and digested food passes through them into the blood, which carries it all over the body. The stomach does the acid soaking, and what is left over goes on to the large intestine, which takes out water and forms solid waste.
questions.grade_note: 5th-grade body units teach that the intestines finish breaking food down so the body can use it, and that the small intestine passes it into the blood (map line G5.L6).

questions.question: The brain is the body's control centre. It sends orders out to the muscles and gets news back from the eyes, ears and skin, all in a flash. What carries these messages?
questions.context: Nerves are thread-like bundles that branch out from the brain and spinal cord to every part of the body, carrying news in and orders out. Veins carry blood back to the heart, tendons tie muscles to bones, and ligaments tie bones to other bones.
questions.grade_note: The brain as the control centre and the nerves as its messengers are taught in Core Knowledge's grade 3 nervous-system unit and reviewed in 5th-grade body units (map line G5.L6).

questions.question: Bones hold the body up and give it its shape. Some bones also form hard cases around soft organs inside. Which bones guard the brain?
questions.context: The skull, 22 bones joined together, forms a hard case around the brain. The ribs make a cage around the heart and lungs, and the spine guards the spinal cord, the pathway for messages between the brain and the body.
questions.grade_note: That bones support the body and protect organs, the skull the brain and the ribs the heart and lungs, is taught with the skeleton in Core Knowledge grade 3 and reviewed in 5th-grade body units (map line G5.L6).

questions.question: The biceps is a muscle at the front of the upper arm. When it works, the elbow bends and the hand rises toward the shoulder. How does a muscle move a bone?
choices: By sending a signal to it
questions.context: A working muscle gets shorter and pulls on the bone through a cord called a tendon. Muscles can pull but never push, so they work in pairs: the biceps bends the elbow, and the triceps at the back of the arm pulls it straight again. Nerves carry the signal that tells a muscle to work, and the heart does the pumping.
questions.grade_note: Muscles moving bones by pulling, and working in pairs, is taught with the muscular system in Core Knowledge grade 3 and reviewed in 5th-grade body units (map line G5.L6).

questions.question: Every organ in the body has its own job, and some organs are much bigger than others. Which organ is the largest in the human body?
questions.context: The skin is the largest organ: an adult's weighs nearly 4 kilograms, more than twice as much as the liver, the largest organ inside the body. It covers and protects the whole body, keeping germs out and water in, and it feels heat, cold and touch.
questions.grade_note: The skin as the body's largest organ, covering and protecting it, is a staple fact of 5th-grade body units (map line G5.L6).
